R072-01.notes: Whole passage tracks Marisol learning to swim with Tess. A: Tess teaches 5-year-olds, no competitions, and that's not the focus. C: retirement never discussed. D: dry hometown is one sentence of background.

R072-02.notes: P1: grew up in a dry inland town (only a cattle tank); by the time she reached the coast 'the moment for learning seemed to have passed.' B: no fear of the tank stated. C: bus job is not given as the cause. D: no mention of lack of invitations; Tess does invite her in.

R072-03.notes: Excuses are refuted (82 degrees, suit under dress), and the pause leads Tess to ask whether she can swim; they are evasions. A: no crowds/dislike. B: she is wearing the suit; the excuse is a pretext. C: nothing suggests she wants to leave.

R072-04.notes: 'Carrying a heavy bag for years and someone had finally offered to take one handle' = long-held burden eased by sharing; she feels relief. A: literal misreading. B: no family-secrecy duty. D: contradicts 'relief.'

R072-05.notes: Light teasing to make lessons seem doable; Marisol replies in kind ('You'd be surprised'). A: not serious criticism. C: no complaint about students. D: she is offering, not refusing.

R072-06.notes: P4: 'float on her back while Tess kept one hand flat beneath her shoulders.' B: 'Tess did not push.' C: kicking holding the wall; shallow end mentioned, not deep end. D: students not involved in lessons.

R072-07.notes: 'The kind of thing people said to five-year-olds, but she noticed that it worked anyway.' A: she kept learning. C: overstates. D: no such history.

R072-08.notes: Simile pairs with 'slowly' and 'She was not graceful': careful, deliberate, determined, not easy. A: contradicts 'slowly'; bus pun is a trap. B: 'chin held high' tempts as pride, but the show-off moment is a later scene and the simile describes her ordinary swimming. D: a person crossing a busy street is attentive, not careless.

R072-09.notes: Tess's question (P2) precedes the lessons (P4) and the final-Saturday swim with watching children (P5). B, A, C all follow D.

R072-10.notes: She arrived early and links 'never late' to swimming the length before the class: same pride in punctuality/reliability she had as a driver. B: no regret expressed. C: no return to work. D: she does not dispute 'show-off'; her quip accepts the teasing.

R072-11.notes: Passage surveys dolphins, ducks, seals, frigatebirds and ends with open questions about sleep. A: no such argument. B: methods only incidental. D: hunting never discussed.

R072-12.notes: P1: 'the eye connected to the waking half of the brain typically stays open, and the dolphin keeps swimming.' A: one eye open. C: that is the fur seal. D: describes unihemispheric, not whole-brain.

R072-13.notes: P2: end ducks 'more often slept with one half of the brain awake.' A: duration not compared. B: reversed (they kept open the eye facing away). C: 'never' overstates 'more often.'

R072-14.notes: P2: eye facing away, 'toward the direction from which a predator would most likely approach.' B, C, D: unsupported.

R072-15.notes: P3: both halves on land; 'at sea, however, they mostly use unihemispheric sleep.' A: reversed. B, D: not mentioned.

R072-16.notes: Topic sentence of P3: 'Some animals change the way they sleep depending on their surroundings,' with seals as the example. A: they sleep both halves on land. C: that is P2. D: no comparison of amounts.

flags.note: Overlaps with R072-18: R072-18's key ('brief bursts') and the same paragraph cue R072-17. Minor cross-item redundancy, not a defect in either key.

R072-17.notes: About 40 min/day in flight vs more than 12 hours on land. A, B: contradicted. C: on-land hemisphere pattern not stated; the 'one half' detail concerns flight.

R072-18.notes: P4: 'sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both, but only in brief bursts.' B: they did sleep. C: 'never with both' contradicted. D: brief bursts, not long periods.

R072-19.notes: Final sentence: 'no one knows how the birds manage on so little sleep.' A: answered in P1. B: answered by the 2016 study (it was the old question). D: answered in P3 (at sea).

R072-20.notes: 'The most dramatic example' = most striking/remarkable. A, C: stage or feeling senses do not fit a scientific example. D: 'sudden' does not fit.
